documents.title: Write-up: Client Onboarding Triage Agent
documents.text:
CLIENT ONBOARDING TRIAGE AGENT
Case study submission — Anika Joshi

The problem I chose, and why it isn't the one in the prompt

The brief asks for something that evaluates AI Builder candidates well. I considered building an assessment tool, but I kept returning to what the job description actually rewards: finding a real pain point inside an ambiguous enterprise context and shipping a workflow that respects governance. So my artifact is a working agentic workflow for a problem I know intimately from consulting: client onboarding intake. My claim is that watching me scope, build, and constrain this workflow tells you more about how I would operate as an AI Builder than any quiz could. The onboarding problem is my evidence, not my topic.

Where the pain is

In the firms I've worked with, onboarding a new client means an intake email with attachments, a coordinator re-keying details into the CRM, a compliance checklist, and a kickoff message to the engagement team. Coordinators told me the re-keying alone takes 25 to 40 minutes per client and errors surface weeks later as billing and conflict-check problems. The workflow is repetitive, rule-bound, and full of judgment calls at the edges — exactly the shape where an agent helps with the middle and humans must own the edges.

What I built

An n8n workflow (export attached) that triggers on a new intake submission, parses the attachments, uses Claude to extract a structured client profile (legal name, jurisdiction, entity type, engagement type, key contacts), validates required fields against the intake policy, creates the CRM record, and notifies the onboarding channel with a summary and links. A human reviews every extracted client profile before it enters the CRM — extraction is allowed to be wrong; the record of truth is not. Parsing failures and validation misses route to an exceptions channel with the original documents attached, so nothing silently disappears.

Decision boundaries

I wrote down, before building, which steps the agent owns and which it never will. The agent owns parsing, extraction, formatting, and notification. It does not own conflict checks (regulated judgment), fee arrangements (commercial judgment), or anything that writes to the ledger. Those stay human, and the workflow is built so they cannot be reached from the automated path. I think the most important design skill in agentic work is deciding what the agent must never do, and making that structural rather than aspirational.

Data handling

Intake documents contain client PII, so the demo runs entirely on twenty synthetic client profiles I authored by hand — two of them deliberately malformed (a missing jurisdiction, a contact block pasted as an image description) to exercise the exception path. In a real deployment the extraction call would run inside the firm's approved environment, not a public endpoint, and the intake bucket would carry the same retention policy as the matter file. I tested the happy path and both exception paths against all twenty profiles before recording the demo.

What I left out, on purpose

No OCR for scanned PDFs — the intake form already produces text, and OCR quality problems would have eaten the timebox. No automatic conflict screening — that is a regulated judgment I will not automate on principle. No fine-tuning, no vector store: the extraction prompt plus validation rules handle the variation I could test. With more time I would add a feedback loop from coordinator corrections back into the extraction prompt, because the corrections are the cheapest training data the firm owns.

Risks I'd flag first

The extraction model will eventually produce a confidently wrong legal name; the review step exists for exactly that day. The workflow currently trusts the intake form's claim about entity type more than it should. And adoption risk is real: if the exceptions channel gets noisy, coordinators will stop trusting it — so I capped exceptions at two per run and route the rest to a daily digest instead.

Demo video transcript (excerpt)
documents.text:
[00:00] Hi, I'm walking you through the onboarding triage workflow. I'll submit one of my synthetic intake forms — this one is Meridian Logistics, a fictional freight company.
[00:18] The webhook fires, attachments get parsed, and here's the Claude extraction node returning the structured profile. Notice jurisdiction came back as Ontario and entity type as corporation — both correct for this fixture.
[00:41] Validation passes, the CRM record is created, and the onboarding channel gets the summary with a link to the record.
[00:58] Now the interesting one — I'll submit the malformed fixture with no jurisdiction. Extraction returns null for jurisdiction because the prompt forbids guessing, validation fails it, and it lands in the exceptions channel with the original documents attached. Nothing silently disappears.
[01:22] That's the loop. The parts I didn't automate — conflict checks and fee arrangements — aren't reachable from this path at all, which I think matters more than any prompt instruction.
